blocks.content: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Matrices are fundamental tools for representing linear transformations and systems of equations.

Notation

An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. For example, a 2×3 matrix:

Matrix Addition

Two matrices of the same size are added element-wise:
\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} e & f \\ g & h \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a+e & b+f \\ c+g & d+h \end{bmatrix}

Matrix Multiplication

To multiply A × B, the number of columns in A must equal the number of rows in B. Each entry of the result is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B.

The Determinant

For a 2×2 matrix, the determinant measures the scaling factor of the linear transformation — and whether it preserves orientation.
\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc
If the determinant is 0, the matrix is singular — it collapses space into a lower dimension and has no inverse.

blocks.question: What is the size of the resulting matrix when you multiply a 3×4 matrix by a 4×2 matrix?
blocks.explanation: A (3×4) × (4×2) multiplication gives a 3×2 result. The inner dimensions (4) must match; the outer dimensions (3 and 2) become the result size.

Matrix multiplication is generally:
options: Not commutative — AB ≠ BA in general
Always undefined unless matrices are square
blocks.explanation: Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative in general. Even when both AB and BA are defined, they may produce different results.
